title: The Gait That Changed After Suppression — Late Efavirenz Cerebellar Ataxia Despite HIV Suppression, CYP2B6 Poor Metabolizers & NNRTI Allosteric Pocket

teenKit.tldr: A life-saving HIV drug successfully cleared a patient's virus for three years, but a hidden genetic quirk caused the medicine to build up in her body and slowly wreck her balance. This medical mystery proves that a treatment can crush a disease while accidentally sabotaging the human host.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It changes how we view medicine by proving that a cure is only as good as the individual patient's unique DNA, showing why the future of health care must be completely personalized.
keyTakeaways: Even when a drug successfully destroys a pathogen, it can still cause severe side effects if it accumulates in the body over time.
A person's genetic makeup—specifically how fast their liver enzymes break down chemicals—determines whether a standard drug dose is helpful or toxic.
Tiny, one-angstrom changes in molecular structures and protein pockets dictate how drugs interact with our cells and cause unexpected physical symptoms.

vocab.meaning: A medical condition affecting the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination, leading to clumsy movements or an unsteady walk.
A genetic variation where a person's liver processes specific drugs much slower than usual, causing the medication to build up to dangerous levels in the blood.
A specialized tiny cavity or shape on the surface of a protein where molecules can bind to alter the protein's behavior.
The study of how an individual's unique genetic code affects their body's response to specific medications.

quiz.question: What was the ultimate clinical paradox presented by the patient's case?
options: The drug cured the virus, but the virus mutated and fought back.
The drug successfully crushed the virus for three years while slowly damaging her nervous system and balance.
The patient refused to take the medication, yet her viral load dropped to zero.
The medication caused severe hair loss but instantly cured her ataxia.
quiz.explanation: The paradox highlights how a treatment can completely achieve its goal against an infection while paradoxically harming the host through a delayed toxic side effect.

quiz.question: Why did the medication build up to toxic levels in this specific patient over three years?
options: She was taking ten times the normal daily dosage.
She had a genetic liver enzyme variation that made her a poor metabolizer of the drug.
The virus learned how to trap the medication inside her brain cells.
Her kidneys stopped functioning completely on day one.
quiz.explanation: Her genetic profile as a CYP2B6 poor metabolizer meant her liver cleared the drug far too slowly, causing it to accumulate over time.

quiz.question: What microscopic scale did investigators have to analyze to understand how the drug interacted with biological machinery?
quiz.explanation: Scientists zoomed down to the hyper-precise one-angstrom scale to study the exact atomic geometry of the protein pocket where the drug binds.
